Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

Inputs in the top half don’t have seeds, but rows 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, and 11 fill with 9s, reflecting seed rows across row 12. The lower part, row 13 seed c3, might align with rows 1 and 2. I think the output in the top area might involve bands of 9, reflecting lines from 9 pixels below.

# Continual-ARC reusable observation

## Verified resolution: directional L recoloring (task-0fdb20b5)
This task was correctly solved on a 15x29 test after two demos. The input had background 5 and a large color-2 L marker near the upper-right: vertical arm in column 22 at rows 0-5, horizontal arm along row 5 columns 22-28. The only change in the correct output was recoloring the connected color-0 component at rows 2-5, columns 16-18 from 0 to 2; every other cell stayed exactly as input. That component is 3x3 at rows 2-4 (with row 5 columns 16-17) and connected as one object. Preserve the grid dimensions; leave the marker and all other components untouched.

The two demos confirm the general output form: exactly one object changes uniformly into the L marker's color. Demo 1: color-2 L marker, target color-1 component at rows 16-19 cols 5-7 recolored to 2. Demo 2: color-7 L marker, target color-2 object at rows 0-3 cols 0-5 recolored to 7. The target selector was not fully derived from the examples; therefore retain the solved test as ground truth and avoid unsupported shape/position assumptions. In particular, an earlier note below speculated that a color-3 object in the test was the target; that guess was incorrect. The actual target was the connected color-0 component described above.

## L-marker duplicate-shape recoloring (task-0fdb20b5; inferred from demos, unverified test)
Across demos 6 and 7, a long monochrome L-shaped object acts as a directional marker. Find two congruent (rotation/reflection may count) objects, one on each side of the L's corner/arms; recolor the object on the exterior/opposite side of the L's inner quadrant to the L object's color, leaving everything else unchanged. Strong evidence: demo 7 has color-1 L (vertical upward arm at col 4 and horizontal left arm at row 3), two congruent five-cell shapes (color 8 upper-left and color 6 upper-right); output recolors color-6 object to 1 while preserving color 8. Demo 6 similarly recolors the exterior copy of two matching color-5 blobs to color 6. For this task's test, likely candidate pair: color-3 upper-right L-triomino and the same triomino-like subshape embedded in the lower-right color-8 object; the marker is color-2 L with corner at row 6,col 12 and arms extending right/down, so likely recolor the external color-3 upper-right object to 2. ## Detailed observations: task-0fdb20b5 demos (all eight)
Input/output dimensions are identical in every pair; every pixel is preserved except one connected object, recolored uniformly to the color of a large L-shaped line/bar marker. This is the high-confidence common rule; target selection depends on a geometric relation that was not fully resolved during the instance. Record the differences exactly:
- Demo 1, 24x18, background 3: a small color-6 L triomino at rows 12-13, cols 9-10 (0-indexed) becomes 0. Other cells unchanged.
- Demo 2, 26x22, background 9: a 2-cell vertical color-8 domino at rows 1-2, col 14 becomes 2. Other cells unchanged.

Do not change any part of the L itself or unrelated objects. In the test (11x17), the marker is color 2: horizontal arm row 6, cols 12-16, vertical arm col 12, rows 6-10. Test other components: color 0 blob rows 1-3 cols 7-9; color 3 domino at rows 1-2 cols 13-14 plus separate vertical domino rows 9-10 col 6; color 4 singleton row 10 col 0; color 8 vertical 4x2 block rows 5-8 cols 2-3, vertical 3-cell at rows 6-8 col 10, and lower-right 7-cell component rows 8-10 cols 14-16. Unresolved target is likely selected by geometry/location relative to the L selector, but the instance ended without a correct submission. Previous attempts mostly changed candidate objects based on unsupported template guesses; retain original dimensions and alter only one whole component when applying a future version of this pattern.

## Enclosed-region fill task (task-46e1e7a4; test ended with all 8 attempts wrong)
Rule from demos: keep grid dimensions and walls, recolor with 4 only the background-color cells enclosed by the line color. The line itself is not recolored. Color values vary; fill is consistently 4.

Examples from this instance:
- Demo 1 (13x21; bg=5, wall=1): fill the 2x3 pocket at rows 2-3, cols 3-5 (0-indexed).
- Demo 2 (10x27; bg=8, wall=9): fill 2x3 pockets at rows 4-5, cols 4-6 and cols 16-18.
- Demo 3 (10x13; bg=5, wall=1): fill row 5, cols 1-4.
- Demo 4 (29x21; bg=9, wall=0): fill enclosed rectangles rows 2-3, cols 2-4 and cols 17-19, plus rows 8-9, cols 3-4 and cols 13-14, and rows 8-9, col 18.

Operational rule: flood-fill background from the grid perimeter using 4-neighbor adjacency; convert only unreachable background cells to 4. Preserve all walls and exterior cells. Consider the grid edge as a possible boundary only where the wall arrangement closes a pocket against it; do not assume regions touching an edge are always exterior without tracing openings.

Test input for this instance (20x25; bg=2, wall=8) was submitted incorrectly eight times. The wall path has vertical segments at c22 (r0-4), c21 (r4-9), horizontal walls r4 c21-24, r7 c0-21, r9 c21-24, then c22 r9-19. Many guessed fills at right-side areas were wrong; a standard perimeter flood fill appears to imply no enclosed background pockets and thus unchanged grid, but this was not validated by a correct result. ## Separator-grid tile counting (validated, task-56550ab9)

A grid can be partitioned by full horizontal/vertical separator lines of a distinctive color. Ignore separators and treat the resulting equal-sized tiles independently. Count occurrences of the tile's non-background/special color; encode the tile as `1` iff the count is exactly 2, otherwise output the background color. Output dimensions equal the number of tile rows by tile columns.

Evidence:
- Demo 1: separator color 7, background 2, special 9; separators at row 4 and columns 2,5,8,11 (0-indexed), forming 2x5 tiles each 4x2. Output is 2x5; only top-left tile has output 2 because it has exactly one special 9, whereas all other tiles output 1. This is inconsistent with the general rule above as written; actually outputs show **background color for exactly one special**, and 1 otherwise. Check demo 2 to resolve: Demo 2 background 9 / special 4, tiles 4x3; outputs 1 where count=2, 9 for count=0 or 1. Therefore the per-task encoding differs, or demo1's output is explained by the count relation: special color 9 and background 2, output=1 for count >=2, else background 2. Adopt robust observed encoding: in demo1, output 2 for count=1 and 1 for count>=2; in demo2, output 1 for count=2 and 9 for count !=2.
- Validated test: separators color 3 at full rows 3,7 and columns 4,9, creating 3x3 tiles, each 3x4. Background 6, special 5. Tile special-color counts by row: `[2,1,2]`, `[1,2,1]`, `[2,2,2]`. Output was correctly submitted as `[[1,6,1],[6,1,6],[1,1,1]]`; thus for this test the mapping is 1 iff the tile has exactly two 5s, otherwise background 6.

Practical approach: identify full-line separators and crop tiles; use demos to establish the encoding exactly, since rule mapping differed across the two examples above. Avoid guessing output dimensions or treating inputs as a single undivided grid. Preserve no input tile pixels in output; output is a compact matrix of tile classifications.

## Pattern-copy/recolor rule (validated by demonstrations in task-b2328396)

When a grid contains a small connected colored seed object amid a background/noise grid, locate translations of the seed's exact pixel mask where every seed-mask position is zero. Recolor the matched mask pixels to the seed color. For the observed task, matches were in the **same orientation only** (no rotations/reflections); cells outside the mask's bounding box are unconstrained, so do not require holes/complement positions to equal the background. Allow overlapping occurrences and take the union of all matched mask cells. Preserve all other cells, including the original seed.

Evidence: Demo pair 5's seed color-2 mask had offsets `[(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1)]` (relative to its top-left). Searching translations in that same orientation, requiring only mask cells to be zero, gave 16 matches and their union exactly equaled all output changes. Other orientations did not match the demonstrated output. Demo pair 3 similarly validated same-orientation translated mask matching without constraints on bounding-box holes.

For task-b2328396 specifically, the seed was color 8 with offsets `[(0,0),(0,1),(1,0)]` (the top-left three cells of a 2x2 box). Mark all translations where those three cells are zero, set them to 8, and leave the fourth corner unconstrained. This exact method ultimately solved the instance. Earlier mistakes came from trying larger/incorrect masks, rotations, or imposing a condition on the fourth corner/background.
